Medicine-4.question: ১) Which is the most important risk factor for duodenal ulcer?
Medicine-4.exp:
The most important risk factor for duodenal ulcer is Helicobacter pylori infection.

H. pylori causes:

  • Increased gastric acid secretion (especially via increased gastrin release)

  • Reduced duodenal mucosal protection

  • Gastric metaplasia in the duodenum, allowing bacterial colonization and ulcer formation

Other options:

  • NSAIDs → Important cause of peptic ulcers, especially gastric ulcers, but the strongest association for duodenal ulcer is H. pylori.

  • Smoking → Increases risk and delays ulcer healing but is not the primary factor.

  • Spicy foods → May worsen dyspeptic symptoms but do not cause duodenal ulcers.

Exam pearl:
Duodenal ulcer → Most common association: H. pylori infection.
Gastric ulcer → Think NSAIDs + H. pylori.

Medicine-4.question: ২) Gastric erosions & ulcers are differentiated from each other on the basis of their penetration into.......?
Medicine-4.exp:
The difference between gastric erosion and gastric ulcer is based on the depth of mucosal injury:

  • Gastric erosion → Superficial mucosal defect that does not extend beyond the muscularis mucosa.

  • Gastric ulcer → A deeper lesion that extends through the muscularis mucosa into the submucosa or deeper layers.

Other options:

  • Muscularis interna → Not the standard anatomical layer used for this distinction.

  • Muscularis externa → Involvement indicates a very deep penetrating lesion, not the basic definition.

  • Submucosa → Ulcers extend into submucosa, but the key dividing line is whether the lesion crosses the muscularis mucosa.

Exam pearl:
Erosion = mucosa only (does not cross muscularis mucosa)
Ulcer = penetrates through muscularis mucosa into submucosa or deeper.

Medicine-4.question: ৩) passage of black, tarry stools containing altered blood is called.... ?
Medicine-4.exp:
Melaena is the passage of black, tarry, foul-smelling stools containing altered blood due to digestion of haemoglobin in the gastrointestinal tract. It usually indicates upper gastrointestinal bleeding, commonly from:

  • Peptic ulcer disease

  • Gastritis

  • Oesophageal varices

Other options:

  • Hematemesis → Vomiting of blood (usually upper GI bleeding).

  • Hematochazia (Hematochezia) → Passage of fresh red blood per rectum, usually from lower GI bleeding.

  • Hemoptysis → Coughing out blood from the respiratory tract.

Exam pearl:
Black tarry stool + altered blood → Melaena → Upper GI bleeding.

Medicine-4.question: ৪) which is a feature of amoebic liver abscess?
Medicine-4.exp:
The characteristic feature of amoebic liver abscess (ALA) is “anchovy sauce” pus, which is a thick brownish material composed of necrotic liver tissue and debris.

Other options:

  • Neutrophilic leukocytosis common → More typical of pyogenic liver abscess; amoebic abscess may show mild leukocytosis.

  • More fatal → Pyogenic liver abscess is generally more severe and has higher mortality compared with amoebic liver abscess.

  • High fever with chills & rigors → More characteristic of pyogenic liver abscess due to bacterial infection.

Exam pearl:
Amoebic liver abscess → Entamoeba histolytica → solitary right lobe lesion → anchovy sauce pus.

Medicine-4.question: ৫) what is the commonest site of gastric ulcer & duodenal ulcer?
Medicine-4.exp:
The commonest sites of peptic ulcers are:

  • Gastric ulcer → Lesser curvature of the stomach (especially near the incisura angularis/antrum region).

  • Duodenal ulcer → First part of the duodenum (duodenal bulb).

Other options:

  • Greater curvature & 2nd part → Not the usual site; ulcers here are uncommon.

  • Lesser curvature & 2nd part → Gastric site is correct, but duodenal site is incorrect.

  • Greater curvature & 1st part → Duodenal site is correct, but gastric site is incorrect.

Exam pearl:
Gastric ulcer → Lesser curvature
Duodenal ulcer → First part (bulb) of duodenum.

Medicine-4.question: ৬) Which is not one of the causes of 90% of cases of acute pancreatitis?
Medicine-4.exp:
About 90% of acute pancreatitis cases are caused by the two most common factors:

  1. Gallstones → Most common cause in many populations due to obstruction of the pancreatic duct by migrating stones.

  2. Alcohol → Major cause, especially in Western countries.

Other recognized causes include:

  • Post-ERCP/MRCP-related pancreatitis → A well-known iatrogenic cause of acute pancreatitis (especially after ERCP).

  • Idiopathic pancreatitis → Accounts for a smaller proportion of cases and is not included among the major causes responsible for 90%.

Exam pearl:
90% acute pancreatitis causes = Gallstones + Alcohol + (drug/ERCP and other recognized causes depending on classification).
Most common causes to remember → Gallstone and Alcohol.

Medicine-4.question: ৭) which is not a cause of fatty liver disease?
Medicine-4.exp:
Fatty liver disease (hepatic steatosis) is commonly associated with metabolic syndrome, which includes:

  • Diabetes mellitus (DM) → Promotes insulin resistance and fat accumulation in the liver.

  • Obesity → Major risk factor for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).

  • Starvation → Can cause fatty liver due to increased fat mobilization and impaired lipid metabolism.

Hypertension (HTN) is a component of metabolic syndrome and is associated with NAFLD, but it is not a direct cause of fatty liver disease.

Other causes of fatty liver include:

  • Alcohol

  • Corticosteroids

  • Malnutrition

  • Rapid weight loss

Exam pearl:
NAFLD risk factors → Obesity + DM + Dyslipidemia + Metabolic syndrome.
Starvation → Can cause fatty liver due to excessive fatty acid mobilization.

Medicine-4.question: ৮) Severe upper abdominal pain in acute pancreatitis usually radiates to the.......?
Medicine-4.exp:
The characteristic pain of acute pancreatitis is severe epigastric (upper abdominal) pain radiating to the back.

Mechanism:

  • The pancreas is a retroperitoneal organ, so inflammation irritates the celiac plexus and retroperitoneal nerves, causing referred pain to the back.

  • Pain is typically constant, severe, and relieved by leaning forward.

Other options:

  • Tip of left shoulder → Seen in diaphragmatic irritation (Kehr’s sign), e.g., splenic rupture.

  • Tip of right shoulder → Can occur with diaphragmatic irritation from hepatobiliary causes.

  • Left arm → More suggestive of cardiac ischemic pain.

Exam pearl:
Acute pancreatitis → Epigastric pain radiating to the back + raised serum amylase/lipase.

Medicine-4.question: ৯) Which is not a inherited liver disease?
Medicine-4.exp:
Budd–Chiari syndrome is not an inherited liver disease. It is caused by obstruction of hepatic venous outflow (hepatic vein or IVC thrombosis), leading to congestive hepatopathy. It is commonly associated with acquired thrombotic conditions such as myeloproliferative disorders and thrombophilia.

Other options are inherited/metabolic liver diseases:

  • Gilbert’s syndrome → Inherited disorder of bilirubin conjugation due to reduced UGT1A1 activity.

  • Wilson’s disease → Autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism (ATP7B mutation).

  • Haemochromatosis → Inherited iron overload disorder (commonly HFE gene mutation).

Exam pearl:
Inherited liver diseases → Gilbert syndrome, Wilson disease, Haemochromatosis.
Budd–Chiari syndrome → Hepatic venous outflow obstruction (acquired).

Medicine-4.question: ১০) which is the most common cystic disease of liver?
Medicine-4.exp:
The most common cystic disease of the liver is a hydatid cyst (echinococcal cyst), caused by Echinococcus granulosus infection.

  • Transmission occurs through ingestion of eggs from infected dogs.

  • The larvae reach the liver via the portal circulation and form cysts.

  • The liver is the most common site of hydatid disease.

Other options:

  • Pseudocyst → Usually associated with the pancreas (pancreatic pseudocyst), not a primary liver cyst.

  • Choledochal cyst → Congenital dilatation of the biliary tree, not the commonest hepatic cystic disease.

  • Pyogenic cyst → Not a typical term; abscesses are infectious collections, not common cystic liver disease.

Exam pearl:
Most common parasitic cyst of liver → Hydatid cyst → Echinococcus granulos

Medicine-4.question: ১১) discoloration of the flanks due to hemorrhagic ascities in acute pancreatitis is called..... ?
Medicine-4.exp:
Grey Turner’s sign is the bluish-purple discoloration of the flanks due to retroperitoneal hemorrhage, classically seen in severe acute pancreatitis (especially hemorrhagic pancreatitis).

Other options:

  • Cullen’s sign → Periumbilical bluish discoloration due to intra-abdominal bleeding (also seen in severe pancreatitis).

  • Murphy’s sign → Pain and arrest of inspiration on palpation of the right upper quadrant; suggests acute cholecystitis.

  • String sign → Radiological/endoscopic sign associated with Crohn’s disease (narrowing of terminal ileum).

Exam pearl:
Acute hemorrhagic pancreatitis:

  • Grey Turner sign → Flank ecchymosis

  • Cullen sign → Periumbilical ecchymosis.

Medicine-4.question: ১২) KF rings are found in....?
Medicine-4.exp:
Kayser–Fleischer (KF) rings are a classic feature of Wilson’s disease.

  • Wilson’s disease is an autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism due to mutation of the ATP7B gene.

  • Defective copper excretion causes copper accumulation in tissues, especially:

    • Liver → chronic liver disease/cirrhosis

    • Basal ganglia → neurological symptoms

    • Cornea (Descemet’s membrane) → Kayser–Fleischer rings

Other options:

  • Haemochromatosis → Iron overload disorder (bronze skin, diabetes, liver cirrhosis).

  • Gilbert’s syndrome → Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia due to reduced UGT1A1 activity.

  • Budd–Chiari syndrome → Hepatic venous outflow obstruction.

Exam pearl:
KF ring + liver disease + neurological symptoms → Wilson’s disease (copper accumulation).

Medicine-4.question: ১৩) Which analgesic are usually chosen for acute pancreatitis?
Medicine-4.exp:
In acute pancreatitis, the preferred analgesics are opioids (opiates) because the pain is usually severe and requires strong analgesia.

  • Opiates (e.g., morphine, fentanyl) are commonly used for pain control in acute pancreatitis.

  • Older concerns that morphine causes sphincter of Oddi spasm are not considered a reason to avoid opioids in current practice.

Other options:

  • Steroids → Not used for pain relief in acute pancreatitis.

  • NSAIDs → May be used for mild pain but are usually insufficient for severe pancreatitis pain and may increase GI/renal risks.

  • Non-opiates → Usually inadequate for the severe pain of acute pancreatitis.

Exam pearl:
Acute pancreatitis → Severe epigastric pain → Opioid analgesia is commonly required.

Medicine-4.question: ১৪) which is not a feature of portal hypertension ?
Medicine-4.exp:
Portal hypertension occurs due to increased pressure in the portal venous system and commonly causes:

  • Splenomegaly → Due to congestion of the splenic vein.

  • Ascites → Due to increased portal pressure, reduced albumin synthesis, and sodium/water retention.

  • Variceal bleeding → Due to formation of portosystemic collaterals (especially oesophageal varices).

Gynaecomastia is not a feature of portal hypertension itself. It is a feature of chronic liver disease/cirrhosis due to impaired estrogen metabolism and hormonal imbalance.

Exam pearl:
Portal hypertension features → Splenomegaly + Ascites + Varices.
Gynaecomastia → Cirrhosis stigmata (↑ estrogen effect).

Medicine-4.question: ১৫) Which is not a systemic complications of acute pancreatitis?
Medicine-4.exp:
Pleural effusion is considered a local complication of acute pancreatitis rather than a systemic complication. It occurs due to:

  • Inflammation spreading to the diaphragm

  • Pancreatic fluid leakage into the pleural cavity (especially left-sided effusion)

Systemic complications of acute pancreatitis include:

  • SIRS (Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome) → due to systemic cytokine release.

  • Hypoxia → due to pulmonary complications such as ARDS.

  • Hyperglycemia → due to pancreatic endocrine dysfunction and stress response.

Exam pearl:
Acute pancreatitis complications:

  • Systemic: SIRS, ARDS/hypoxia, shock, renal failure, hyperglycemia.

  • Local: Pancreatic necrosis, pseudocyst, abscess, pleural effusion.

Medicine-4.question: ১৬) Which is not an adverse prognostic factors in acute pancreatitis?
Medicine-4.exp:
Adverse prognostic factors in acute pancreatitis are assessed by scoring systems like Ranson’s criteria and Glasgow-Imrie score.

Important poor prognostic indicators include:

  • Age >55 years ✅

  • Blood glucose >10 mmol/L ✅

  • Urea >7 mmol/L ✅ (marker of dehydration/renal impairment and severity)

ALT >200 U/L is not a prognostic factor for severity of acute pancreatitis. However, a raised ALT (>150 U/L) can suggest a biliary cause (gallstone pancreatitis).

Exam pearl:
Acute pancreatitis severity markers → Age, WBC, glucose, urea, calcium, PaO₂, albumin, LDH, AST.
ALT elevation → points toward gallstone etiology, not severity.

Medicine-4.question: ১৭) which cell plays key role in pathogenesis of liver cirrhosis?
Medicine-4.exp:
The key cell involved in the pathogenesis of liver cirrhosis is the Ito cell (hepatic stellate cell).

  • Ito cells are located in the space of Disse and, when activated by chronic liver injury, transform into myofibroblast-like cells.

  • They produce excessive collagen and extracellular matrix, causing hepatic fibrosis and eventually cirrhosis.

Other options:

  • Hepatocyte → Main functional cell of the liver; injury contributes to cirrhosis but is not the key fibrogenic cell.

  • Sinusoidal cell → Not the primary driver of fibrosis.

  • Kupffer cell → Liver macrophages that release cytokines and activate stellate cells, but they do not directly produce most collagen.

Exam pearl:
Liver fibrosis/cirrhosis → activation of Ito (hepatic stellate) cells → collagen deposition.

Medicine-4.question: ১৮) What is the cause of recurrrent & severe acute pancreatitis?
Medicine-4.exp:
Hereditary pancreatitis is an important cause of recurrent and severe acute pancreatitis, especially when attacks occur at a young age or repeatedly without common causes.

  • It is usually due to genetic mutations such as:

    • PRSS1 mutation → increased activation of trypsinogen to trypsin.

    • SPINK1/CFTR mutations → impaired pancreatic protection.

Other options:

  • Alcohol → A common cause of acute and chronic pancreatitis, but not the classic cause of recurrent severe attacks in younger patients.

  • Tobacco → Risk factor for chronic pancreatitis and pancreatic cancer, but less specific.

  • Post-necrotic → Not a primary cause of recurrent severe acute pancreatitis.

Exam pearl:
Recurrent severe acute pancreatitis in young patients → Think hereditary pancreatitis (PRSS1 mutation).

Medicine-4.question: ১৯) what is the route for transmission of hepatitis A?
Medicine-4.exp:
Hepatitis A virus (HAV) is transmitted mainly by the feco-oral route.

Transmission occurs when a person ingests food or water contaminated with feces containing HAV. It is commonly associated with:

  • Poor sanitation

  • Contaminated food/water

  • Close household contact

Other options:

  • Blood → Typical route for HBV, HCV, not HAV.

  • Sexual contact → Can occur (especially oral-anal contact), but not the main route.

  • Saliva → Not a recognized route of HAV transmission.

Exam pearl:
HAV → Feco-oral transmission → Acute hepatitis → No chronic infection.

Medicine-4.question: ২০) Which is the gold standard but invasive & seldom used test of pancreatic function?
Medicine-4.option2: collection of pure pancreatic juice after secretin injection
Medicine-4.exp:
The cause of recurrent and severe acute pancreatitis is classically hereditary pancreatitis.

  • Hereditary pancreatitis occurs due to genetic mutations, most commonly:

    • PRSS1 mutation → premature activation of trypsinogen inside the pancreas.

    • SPINK1/CFTR mutations → increased susceptibility to pancreatic injury.

  • It often presents with recurrent episodes of severe acute pancreatitis and may progress to chronic pancreatitis.

Other options:

  • Alcohol → Common cause of acute and chronic pancreatitis, but not the classic cause of recurrent severe attacks, especially in young patients.

  • Tobacco → Risk factor for chronic pancreatitis and pancreatic cancer.

  • Post-necrotic → Not a primary cause of recurrent acute pancreatitis.

Exam pearl:
Young patient + recurrent severe pancreatitis → Think hereditary pancreatitis (PRSS1 mutation).

Medicine-4.question: ২১) which is not a test for diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis?
Medicine-4.exp:
Serum amylase is not a reliable test for diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis.

  • In chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic tissue is progressively destroyed, so enzyme production decreases. Therefore, serum amylase may be normal or only mildly elevated and has poor diagnostic value.

Useful investigations for chronic pancreatitis include:

  • USG → May show pancreatic calcification, duct dilatation, or structural changes.

  • Abdominal X-ray → Can detect pancreatic calcifications (classical finding).

  • MRCP → Non-invasive assessment of pancreatic duct abnormalities.

Exam pearl:
Chronic pancreatitis → Abdominal X-ray showing pancreatic calcification is highly suggestive; serum amylase is often normal.

Medicine-4.question: ২২) Which is not true about hemolytic jaundice?
Medicine-4.exp:
In hemolytic jaundice (pre-hepatic jaundice), excessive breakdown of RBCs causes increased production of unconjugated bilirubin.

Features:

  • Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia  (not conjugated)

  • ALP normal  (bile ducts are not obstructed)

  • AST usually normal  (no primary hepatocyte injury)

  • Stercobilinogen increased  due to increased bilirubin delivery to the intestine and increased conversion to stercobilin.

Other option:

  • Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia  → Seen mainly in obstructive jaundice and hepatocellular jaundice, not hemolytic jaundice.

Exam pearl:
Hemolytic jaundice = ↑ unconjugated bilirubin + ↑ urine/stool urobilinogen (stercobilinogen) + normal ALP.

Medicine-4.question: ২৩) which is a cause of tender hepatomegaly?
Medicine-4.exp:
Budd–Chiari syndrome is a classic cause of tender hepatomegaly.

  • It occurs due to hepatic venous outflow obstruction (hepatic vein/IVC thrombosis), causing:

    • Congestion of blood in the liver

    • Rapid enlargement of the liver

    • Painful/tender hepatomegaly

    • Ascites and liver dysfunction

Other options:

  • Malaria → May cause hepatosplenomegaly, but liver is usually not markedly tender.

  • Kala azar (visceral leishmaniasis) → Causes massive splenomegaly and hepatomegaly, usually non-tender.

  • Lymphoma → Can cause hepatomegaly, generally non-tender.

Exam pearl:
Tender hepatomegaly → Think acute congestion/inflammation: Budd–Chiari syndrome, acute hepatitis, liver abscess, CCF.

Medicine-4.question: ২৪) All of the following drugs causes acute liver failure except....?
Medicine-4.exp:
Among the given drugs, nitrous oxide is not a cause of acute liver failure.

Causes of drug-induced acute liver failure include:

  • Paracetamol (acetaminophen)  → Most common cause of acute liver failure due to overdose.

  • Anti-TB drugs (especially isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide) → Can cause hepatotoxicity.

  • Halothane  → Can cause halothane hepatitis (immune-mediated severe hepatic necrosis).

Nitrous oxide  → It is not typically associated with acute liver failure.

Exam pearl:
Acute liver failure drug causes → Paracetamol, Anti-TB drugs, Halothane.
Most common drug cause worldwide → Paracetamol overdose.

Medicine-4.question: ২৫) which is not a usual consequence of H. pylori infection?
Medicine-4.exp:
Helicobacter pylori infection is strongly associated with:

  • Duodenal ulcer  → H. pylori is the most important cause.

  • Gastric ulcer  → Due to chronic gastritis and mucosal damage.

  • Gastric cancer  → Especially non-cardia gastric adenocarcinoma (H. pylori is a Class I carcinogen).

  • MALT lymphoma → Also associated with chronic H. pylori infection.

Duodenal cancer  is not a usual consequence of H. pylori infection.

Exam pearl:
H. pylori → Duodenal ulcer + Gastric ulcer + Gastric adenocarcinoma + MALT lymphoma.

Medicine-4.question: ২৬) Which type of tremor of the extended hand is found in acute liver failure?
Medicine-4.exp:
The tremor seen when a patient with acute liver failure extends their hands is called a flapping tremor (asterixis).

  • Asterixis is a type of negative myoclonus characterized by brief lapses of muscle tone causing a “flapping” movement of the hands when the arms are extended and wrists are dorsiflexed.

  • It occurs due to hepatic encephalopathy caused by accumulation of neurotoxins (especially ammonia).

Other options:

  • Resting tremor → Seen in Parkinson’s disease.

  • Intention tremor → Seen in cerebellar lesions (worsens as the target is approached).

  • Action tremor → Occurs during voluntary movement, e.g., essential tremor.

Exam pearl:
Acute liver failure → Hepatic encephalopathy → Asterixis (flapping tremor).

Medicine-4.question: ২৭) inability to perform simple mental arithmetic tasks or draw objects such as stars found in hepatic encephalopathy is called....?
Medicine-4.exp:
The inability to perform simple mental arithmetic tasks or draw objects such as stars in hepatic encephalopathy is called constructional apraxia.

  • Constructional apraxia is a cognitive impairment where the patient cannot correctly copy or construct figures due to impaired visuospatial ability. It is assessed by tasks like drawing a star, cube, or clock.

  • It is a feature of hepatic encephalopathy due to impaired cerebral function from accumulation of toxins (especially ammonia).

Other options:

  • Asterixis → Flapping tremor due to negative myoclonus in hepatic encephalopathy.

  • Hyperreflexia → May occur in advanced hepatic encephalopathy but not related to drawing/calculation difficulty.

  • Fetor hepaticus → Musty, sweet breath odor due to volatile sulfur compounds.

Exam pearl:
Hepatic encephalopathy signs:

  • Asterixis → flapping tremor

  • Constructional apraxia → inability to draw figures

  • Fetor hepaticus → characteristic breath odor.

Medicine-4.question: ২৮) which is not true about hepatocellular jaundice?
Medicine-4.exp:
In hepatocellular jaundice, the main problem is damage to hepatocytes, causing leakage of intracellular enzymes and impaired liver synthetic function.

Features include:

  • High rise of AST  → Due to hepatocyte injury.

  • High rise of ALT  → More specific marker of hepatocellular damage.

  • Prolonged PT  → Due to reduced synthesis of clotting factors by the damaged liver.

High rise of ALP  is not typical of hepatocellular jaundice. It is more characteristic of cholestatic/obstructive jaundice due to bile duct obstruction.

Exam pearl:
Hepatocellular jaundice → ↑ ALT/AST + ↑ PT (↓ synthetic function).
Cholestatic jaundice → ↑ ALP + ↑ GGT.

Medicine-4.question: ২৯) In hepatic encephalopathy EEG shows diffuse slowing of normal..... waves?
Medicine-4.exp:
In hepatic encephalopathy, EEG shows diffuse slowing of normal alpha waves due to impaired cerebral function caused by accumulation of neurotoxins (especially ammonia).

EEG changes in hepatic encephalopathy include:

  • ↓ Frequency of alpha rhythm

  • Increased theta and delta activity (slowing pattern)

  • In severe cases → triphasic waves may appear

Other options:

  • Beta waves → Associated with alertness, anxiety, and sedative drug effects.

  • Gamma waves (গুম্মা) → Associated with higher cognitive processing, not hepatic encephalopathy.

  • Delta waves → Slow waves that increase in severe encephalopathy, but the question asks the normal wave that becomes slowed.

Exam pearl:
Hepatic encephalopathy EEG → diffuse slowing of alpha rhythm + triphasic waves.

Medicine-4.question: ৩০) which of the following is not a precipitating factor of hepatic encephalopathy?
Medicine-4.exp:
Common precipitating factors of hepatic encephalopathy include conditions that increase ammonia production or reduce its clearance:

  • Constipation ✅ → Increased intestinal ammonia absorption due to prolonged bacterial action on stool.

  • Dehydration ✅ → Causes reduced renal clearance and precipitates encephalopathy.

  • Infection ✅ → Increases catabolism and inflammatory response, raising ammonia levels.

  • Hypokalemia (low potassium) is a precipitating factor ❗ because it promotes renal ammoniagenesis.

Hyperkalemia  is not a usual precipitating factor of hepatic encephalopathy.

Exam pearl:
Hepatic encephalopathy triggers: “A few C’s” → Constipation, Cirrhosis bleeding (GI bleed), Crisis/infection, Creatinine/renal failure, and low potassium.

Medicine-4.question: ৩১) Which is not a feature of pain of PUD?
Medicine-4.exp:
Pain of peptic ulcer disease (PUD) is typically epigastric pain with a characteristic relationship to meals and an episodic pattern.

Features:

  • Epigastric pain  → Most common presentation.

  • Episodic occurrence  → Pain often occurs in episodes, especially with ulcer activity.

  • Relationship with food → Usually present:

    • Duodenal ulcer → Pain occurs 2–5 hours after meals and improves with food.

    • Gastric ulcer → Pain may worsen after eating.

  • Radiation to back  → Not a usual feature of PUD; it is more suggestive of pancreatitis or penetrating posterior ulcers.

Exam pearl:
PUD pain = Epigastric + episodic + meal-related.
Pain radiating to back → Think acute pancreatitis.

Medicine-4.question: ৩২) which is a cause of hepatic bruit?
Medicine-4.exp:
A hepatic bruit is an uncommon but important clinical sign caused by increased arterial blood flow through the liver, classically seen in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

  • HCC → Tumor vascularity and arteriovenous shunting produce a systolic hepatic bruit.

  • CLD (Chronic liver disease) → May cause cirrhosis and portal hypertension but does not usually produce a hepatic bruit.

  • CCF (Congestive cardiac failure) → Causes congestive hepatomegaly, not hepatic bruit.

  • Liver abscess → May cause tender hepatomegaly and fever, but not bruit.

Exam pearl:
Hepatic bruit → Think HCC (highly vascular liver tumor).

Medicine-4.question: ৩৩) Which is a non invasive test for H. pylori detection?
Medicine-4.exp:
The urea breath test is a non-invasive test used for detection of Helicobacter pylori infection.

  • H. pylori produces the enzyme urease, which breaks down labeled urea into CO₂ + ammonia. The labeled CO₂ is detected in the patient's breath.

Other options:

  • Histology  → Invasive; requires endoscopic gastric biopsy.

  • Rapid urease test (CLO test) → Invasive; requires gastric biopsy during endoscopy.

  • Microbiological culture  → Invasive; requires biopsy specimen.

Exam pearl:
Non-invasive H. pylori tests → Urea breath test + stool antigen test.
Invasive tests → Histology, rapid urease test, culture (all require biopsy).

Medicine-4.question: ৩৪) All of the following group of drugs are to be avoided in cirrhosis except....?
Medicine-4.exp:
In liver cirrhosis, several drugs should be avoided because they can worsen complications like hepatic encephalopathy, renal failure, and fluid imbalance.

  • NSAIDs → Avoid because they reduce renal blood flow, increase risk of hepatorenal syndrome, and worsen ascites.

  • Narcotics  → Avoid because they can precipitate or worsen hepatic encephalopathy due to CNS depression.

  • Anxiolytics  → Especially benzodiazepines should be avoided as they may trigger hepatic encephalopathy.

  • Diuretics  → Used commonly in cirrhosis with ascites (e.g., spironolactone ± furosemide).

Exam pearl:
Cirrhosis with ascites → Spironolactone is first-line therapy.
Avoid → NSAIDs + sedatives (narcotics/benzodiazepines).

Medicine-4.question: ৩৫) which is a elective indication of Surgery in PUD?
Medicine-4.exp:
Gastric outflow obstruction is an elective indication for surgery in peptic ulcer disease (PUD).

  • Chronic duodenal or pyloric ulcers can cause fibrosis and scarring, leading to gastric outlet obstruction (pyloric stenosis). These patients may require elective surgical intervention.

Other options:

  • Perforation → Usually requires emergency surgery due to acute abdomen and peritonitis.

  • Hemorrhage → Usually managed initially by endoscopic therapy; surgery is considered if bleeding is uncontrolled (often urgent/emergency).

  • GERD → Not an indication for surgery in PUD.

Exam pearl:
PUD surgery indications:

  • Emergency → Perforation, uncontrolled bleeding

  • Elective → Gastric outlet obstruction, intractable/refractory ulcer, suspicion of malignancy.

Medicine-4.question: ৩৬) which is true about obstructive jaundice?
Medicine-4.exp:
In obstructive jaundice (cholestatic jaundice), obstruction of bile flow causes reduced absorption of fat-soluble vitamin K, leading to impaired synthesis of clotting factors and prolonged prothrombin time (PT).

Features of obstructive jaundice:

  • PT prolonged → due to vitamin K deficiency.

  • ALP markedly increased → most characteristic enzyme rise.

  • ALT and AST may rise mildly but are not typically very high.

  • ALP normal is incorrect.

Other options:

  • ALT high rise → More typical of hepatocellular injury (e.g., acute viral hepatitis).

  • AST high rise → Seen in hepatocellular damage.

  • ALP normal → Not seen in obstruction.

Exam pearl:
Obstructive jaundice → ↑ ALP + ↑ GGT + prolonged PT (corrects with vitamin K).

Medicine-4.question: ৩৭) which is the commonest site for abdominal tuberculosis?
Medicine-4.exp:
The ileocecal region is the commonest site of abdominal tuberculosis.

Reasons:

  • It has a high concentration of lymphoid tissue (Peyer’s patches), which favors implantation of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

  • It has relatively slower intestinal transit, allowing more time for bacterial contact with mucosa.

Other options:

  • 2nd part of duodenum → Rare site for intestinal TB.

  • Jejunum → Less commonly affected.

  • Colic flexure → Uncommon site.

Exam pearl:
Intestinal tuberculosis → Most common site: Ileocecal junction.

Medicine-4.question: ৩৮) which hepatitis virus infection can be fulminant during prrgnancy?
Medicine-4.exp:
Hepatitis E virus (HEV) infection can become fulminant during pregnancy, especially in the third trimester.

  • Pregnant women with HEV have a higher risk of:

    • Fulminant hepatic failure

    • Severe jaundice

    • High maternal mortality

Other options:

  • Hepatitis A → Usually acute self-limiting infection; fulminant hepatitis is rare.

  • Hepatitis B → Can cause chronic infection but pregnancy-related fulminant hepatitis is not typical.

  • Hepatitis D → Occurs with HBV infection and can cause severe hepatitis, but not classically associated with pregnancy-related fulminant hepatitis.

Exam pearl:
Pregnancy + fulminant hepatitis → Think Hepatitis E.

Medicine-4.question: ৩৯) which is the anatomical site for ulcerative colitis?
Medicine-4.exp:
Ulcerative colitis (UC) is an inflammatory bowel disease that primarily affects the colon, especially the rectum and extends proximally in a continuous manner.

Key features:

  • Disease is limited to the large intestine (colon).

  • Inflammation involves mainly the mucosa and submucosa.

  • Rectum is almost always involved.

Other options:

  • Duodenum → Not a site of ulcerative colitis.

  • Ileum → Not typically affected (except backwash ileitis in severe pancolitis).

  • Any part of GIT → This is more characteristic of Crohn’s disease, which can affect any part from mouth to anus.

Exam pearl:
Ulcerative colitis → Colon only (continuous lesion, rectum involved).
Crohn’s disease → Any part of GIT (skip lesions).

Medicine-4.question: ৪০) which hepatitis virus has window period?
Medicine-4.exp:
The window period is classically associated with Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection.

  • During the HBV window period, HBsAg has disappeared and anti-HBs has not yet appeared.

  • The most reliable marker during this period is anti-HBc IgM.

Other options:

  • Hepatitis A → Does not have a typical serological window period like HBV.

  • Hepatitis C → Has a period before antibody detection, but the classic “window period” MCQ refers to HBV.

  • Hepatitis E → Acute infection; no classic window period.

Exam pearl:
HBV window period → HBsAg negative + anti-HBs negative + anti-HBc IgM positive.

Medicine-4.question: ৪১) which is not a feature of IBS?
Medicine-4.exp:
Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by abdominal pain associated with altered bowel habits, but it does not cause weight gain as a typical feature.

Typical IBS features:

  • Recurrent abdominal pain

  • Bloating

  • Constipation and/or diarrhea

  • Symptoms related to defecation

The following are alarm features that suggest an organic disease rather than IBS:

  • Anemia

  • Rectal bleeding

  • Nocturnal symptoms

  • Unintentional weight loss

Other options:

  • Anemia → Not a feature of IBS; indicates possible malignancy, IBD, or other pathology.

  • Rectal bleeding → Not typical of IBS.

  • Nocturnal symptoms → Suggest organic disease, not IBS.

Exam pearl:
IBS has no alarm features. Anemia, bleeding, nocturnal symptoms, and weight loss → think organic GI disease.

Medicine-4.question: ৪২) which organism is not a common pathogen for pyogenic liver abscess?
Medicine-4.exp:
Common pathogens causing pyogenic liver abscess include:

  • E. coli → Most common Gram-negative organism.

  • Streptococcus milleri (Streptococcus anginosus group) → Important cause of liver abscess.

  • Bacteroides → Common anaerobic organism, especially from intra-abdominal infections.

Pseudomonas is not a common pathogen of pyogenic liver abscess.

Other important organisms:

  • Klebsiella pneumoniae (especially in diabetic patients)

  • Staphylococcus aureus (less common, associated with bacteremia)

Exam pearl:
Pyogenic liver abscess → E. coli + Klebsiella + Streptococcus milleri + anaerobes (Bacteroides).

Medicine-4.question: ৪৩) which is not a feature of NUD?
Medicine-4.exp:
Non-ulcer dyspepsia (NUD), also called functional dyspepsia, commonly occurs in young patients and presents with upper GI symptoms without an identifiable organic cause.

Features:

  • Patients are usually young → Common in younger age groups.

  • Males are more affected → Seen more commonly in males in many exam references.

  • Bloating after meals → Common symptom due to impaired gastric accommodation and visceral hypersensitivity.

Morning symptoms  are not a typical feature of NUD. Symptoms are usually related to meals and may include postprandial fullness, early satiety, and epigastric discomfort.

Exam pearl:
NUD/Functional dyspepsia → Young patient + post-meal bloating/fullness + epigastric discomfort.

Medicine-4.question: ৪৪) which is not true about pyogenic liver abscess?
Medicine-4.exp:
Pyogenic liver abscess is a serious condition and can be associated with significant morbidity and mortality, especially if untreated. Therefore, “less fatal” is not true.

Features of pyogenic liver abscess:

  • High fever with chills and rigors → Common due to bacterial infection.

  • Frank pus on aspiration → Typical finding; pus is usually thick and purulent.

  • Multiple small lesions on USG → Can occur, especially with biliary or hematogenous spread.

Other point:

  • Amoebic liver abscess usually contains “anchovy sauce” pus and is often a single lesion.

Exam pearl:
Pyogenic liver abscess → High fever + chills/rigors + frank pus + often multiple lesions.

Medicine-4.question: ৪৫) Recurrent abdominal pain in association with abnormal defecation in the absence of a structural abnormality of the gut is called........?
Medicine-4.exp:
Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) is defined as recurrent abdominal pain associated with altered bowel habits (abnormal defecation) in the absence of any structural abnormality of the gut.

Key features of IBS:

  • Recurrent abdominal pain

  • Relation with defecation

  • Altered stool frequency or form (diarrhea, constipation, or both)

  • Normal structural investigations

Other options:

  • IBD (Inflammatory Bowel Disease) → Has structural inflammation of the intestine (e.g., Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis).

  • PUD (Peptic Ulcer Disease) → Causes upper abdominal pain due to gastric/duodenal mucosal ulceration.

  • PID (Pelvic Inflammatory Disease) → Infection/inflammation of female pelvic organs.

Exam pearl:
IBS = Abdominal pain + abnormal defecation + no structural gut disease.

Medicine-4.question: ৪৬) PUD is closely associated with......?
Medicine-4.exp:
Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) is closely associated with Helicobacter pylori infection.

  • H. pylori colonizes the gastric mucosa and causes chronic gastritis.

  • It contributes to ulcer formation by:

    • Increasing gastric acid secretion (especially in duodenal ulcer)

    • Damaging gastric mucosal defenses

    • Producing urease enzyme and inflammatory mediators

Other options:

  • Campylobacter jejuni (C. jejuni) → Causes acute gastroenteritis, not PUD.

  • E. coli → Causes various intestinal infections, not PUD.

  • B. coli → Not a recognized major cause of PUD.

Exam pearl:
Most important associations of PUD → H. pylori infection + NSAID use.

Medicine-4.question: ৪৭) which one is the features of decompensated CLD?
Medicine-4.exp:
Decompensated chronic liver disease (CLD) is characterized by the development of major complications due to loss of liver function.

Features of decompensated CLD include:

  • Jaundice → Due to impaired bilirubin metabolism and excretion.

  • Ascites

  • Variceal bleeding

  • Hepatic encephalopathy

Other options:

  • Fever → Not a defining feature of decompensated CLD; may occur due to infection.

  • Leukonychia → A sign of chronic liver disease but not a decompensation feature.

  • Palmar erythema → A chronic liver disease stigmata, not decompensation.

Exam pearl:
CLD decompensation = “JAVE” → Jaundice + Ascites + Variceal bleeding + Encephalopathy.

Medicine-4.question: ৪৮) which one of the following is a cause of malabsorption syndrome?
Medicine-4.exp:
The most common and classic cause of malabsorption syndrome is coeliac disease.

  • Coeliac disease is an immune-mediated disorder caused by sensitivity to gluten, leading to villous atrophy of the small intestine and impaired absorption of nutrients.

Other options:

  • Acute pancreatitis → Can cause maldigestion during severe pancreatic insufficiency, but acute pancreatitis is not a common cause of chronic malabsorption syndrome.

  • Ulcerative colitis → Mainly affects the colon; malabsorption is not a typical feature.

  • Crohn’s disease → Can cause malabsorption, especially with ileal involvement, but coeliac disease is the classic answer.

Exam pearl:
Malabsorption syndrome → Coeliac disease (villous atrophy + gluten sensitivity).

Medicine-4.question: ৪৯) which is the most common cause of upper GIT bleeding?
Medicine-4.exp:
The most common cause of upper gastrointestinal (UGI) bleeding is bleeding peptic ulcer disease (PUD).

  • Peptic ulcers (especially duodenal ulcers) can erode into blood vessels and cause significant upper GI hemorrhage.

  • Common presentation: hematemesis or melena.

Other options:

  • Oesophageal varices → A major cause of upper GI bleeding in cirrhosis, but not the most common overall.

  • Malignancy → Can cause bleeding but is less common.

  • Mallory–Weiss tear → Causes bleeding after forceful vomiting/retching, but less common.

Exam pearl:
Most common cause of upper GI bleeding → Peptic ulcer disease.
In a cirrhotic patient with UGI bleed → Think oesophageal varices.

Medicine-4.question: ৫০) which type of fever occurs in liver abcess?
Medicine-4.exp:
The typical fever pattern in liver abscess is intermittent fever.

  • Pyogenic liver abscess commonly presents with:

    • High fever

    • Chills and rigors

    • Intermittent fever pattern due to bacteremia and pus formation

Other options:

  • Continued fever → Temperature remains persistently elevated with little variation (e.g., enteric fever).

  • Remittent fever → Temperature fluctuates but does not return to normal.

  • Quotidian fever → Fever occurring every day at a similar time, seen in some infections like malaria patterns.

Exam pearl:
Liver abscess → Intermittent high-grade fever +
